Andrew Lloyd Webber is a British composer who revolutionized musical theatre in the nineteen eighties with a series of commercially colossal productions that blended classical instrumentation, pop sensibility, and theatrical spectacle.

Born in nineteen forty-eight in London, he studied at the Royal College of Music and composed his first musical at age twenty. Evita, released in nineteen seventy-eight and co-written with lyricist Tim Rice, established him as a major force in the industry. A nineteen eighty film adaptation and Broadway success cemented his reputation.

His breakthrough came with Cats in nineteen eighty-one, adapted from T.S. Eliot's poetry collection. It ran for eighteen years on Broadway, making it one of the longest-running musicals ever, and proved that spectacle and individual character could completely trump plot. The Phantom of the Opera, which premiered in nineteen eighty-six, became his masterpiece and the longest-running Broadway musical in history. Its blend of gothic melodrama, soaring tenor vocals, and Puccini-influenced orchestration created a template for modern megamusicals that would define the form for decades.

His compositional signature includes lush orchestrations, memorable melodic hooks accessible to pop audiences, and a recurring use of the pipe organ and classical motifs. Other major works include Sunset Boulevard in nineteen ninety-three and Aspects of Love from nineteen eighty-nine, each exploring different theatrical genres. In more recent years, he composed School of Rock in twenty fifteen.

He won seven Tony Awards and a Grammy. His stage productions have grossed billions of dollars worldwide, making him one of the most financially successful composers in history. His influence on musical theatre economics is immeasurable. His works demonstrated that theatrical blockbusters could achieve film-level box-office returns and cultural penetration, fundamentally reshaping Broadway's investment and production strategies.

He is known for accessibility. His melodies are instantly memorable and singable by amateurs, a characteristic that made his works pervasive in concert halls, school productions, and popular culture far beyond traditional theatre audiences. His compositional method often began with melody first, a departure from the integration of music and text favored by modernist composers, making his works feel immediate and emotionally direct to listeners.

His early career-defining collaboration on Evita with Tim Rice proved his compositional range and ambition. He would go on to create defining works like Cats and The Phantom of the Opera that set the template for modern Broadway blockbusters. In essence, he fundamentally altered the economics and aesthetics of musical theatre in the nineteen eighties and beyond.
